pairs.rationale: The warning not to receive God's grace in vain corresponds to Paul's statement that grace toward him was not empty, followed by his account of labor through God's grace. The exhortation and personal example differ.

Paul quotes the accepted-time/heard-you and salvation-day/helped-you saying and applies its urgency to now. Isaiah's larger unit continues with covenant and restoration promises not reproduced in this quotation.

Both avoid giving cause for stumbling. Here the aim is that the ministry not be blamed; the earlier letter explicitly names Jews, Greeks and God's Church as those toward whom no stumbling should be given.

Both describe ministry through endurance under hardship. Here Paul commends the speakers as God's ministers; the later defense names ministers of Christ and greater labors, imprisonments, beatings and dangers of death. The stated titles remain distinct.

The later hardship catalogue expands beatings, imprisonments, labors, sleeplessness and fastings from this compressed list. It adds counts and dangers, without requiring that every listed hardship be a separate newly identified episode.

Both associate the Spirit with love, patience and kindness. Corinthians's ministry description also includes purity, knowledge and love without hypocrisy; Galatians's fruit list contains further qualities. The lists are related, not identical.

The weapons-of-righteousness image in God's power corresponds to the later weapons that are not fleshly but powerful through God. The later unit does not assign particular weapons to the right and left hands.

Both ministry portraits juxtapose hostile treatment or speech with the workers' actual conduct. Corinthians here includes being regarded as deceivers yet truthful; the earlier letter describes blessing when reviled and appealing when slandered. The descriptions are not identical.

The dying-yet-living paradox corresponds to carrying Jesus' dying in the body so that His life is revealed, and living people being handed over to death for Jesus. This compares the letter's ministry paradoxes, not every accompanying contrast.

Paul's sorrow/joy and poverty/enriching-many contrasts correspond to Macedonian Churches' affliction, abundant joy and deep poverty overflowing in generosity. The Macedonians are different subjects from the ministry speakers here.

The opened-wide heart toward the Corinthians corresponds to the later assurance that they are in the speakers' hearts, to die and live together. These are repeated relational assurances, not a second event.

The claim that constriction lies in the recipients' affections corresponds to Paul's later question whether loving them more means being loved less. Both express perceived asymmetry in affection without identifying every cause.

Open yourselves wide in return corresponds to the later appeal Make room for us. Both ask the Corinthians for a receptive response; the later appeal also denies wronging, corrupting or exploiting anyone.

Both contrast light with darkness in instructions about participation. Ephesians describes the recipients as light in the Lord and forbids sharing darkness's unfruitful works; Corinthians frames incompatible sharing through righteousness/lawlessness and light/darkness. The passages do not supply identical social rules.

The Christ/Beliar and believer/unbeliever contrasts correspond to incompatible participation in the Lord's and demons' cups and tables. The earlier target concerns sacrifices and fellowship with demons; it does not use the name Beliar.

The quotation's walking-among-them and God/people clauses closely correspond to the promise that God will walk among you, be your God and have you as His people. Pronouns change; the dwelling clause is not present in this Leviticus unit.

God's dwelling and the God/people relation correspond to Ezekiel's dwelling promise. Corinthians says in them where Ezekiel says among them; Ezekiel does not include the walking-among-them clause in this unit. These are related components rather than an unchanged reproduction.

The come-out, separation and do-not-touch-unclean clauses correspond to Isaiah's departure instruction. Isaiah addresses those carrying the Lord's vessels; Corinthians applies the language in its temple/people argument and adds reception by the Lord.

The Father/son promise corresponds to God's promise concerning David's royal successor. Corinthians addresses the community as sons and daughters, whereas Samuel speaks of him as son and also discusses discipline. The number, setting and added daughters remain distinct.

These promises points back to God dwelling with His people, receiving them and being their Father. The intervening separation/uncleanness language also prepares the present call to cleansing and holiness. This is the explicit internal premise and consequence.

Make room for us returns to the appeal that the recipients open themselves wide in return. The current statement also denies wronging, corrupting and taking advantage; those denials are not inserted into the earlier unit.

Being in the speakers' hearts corresponds to the earlier heart opened wide toward the Corinthians. The present passage adds dying and living together; the cross-reference does not claim that precise phrase appears in the earlier assurance.

Paul's fullness of comfort amid affliction corresponds to the opening account of God comforting the speakers in all their affliction. The present unit adds overflowing joy and boldness toward the recipients.

The earlier travel account describes unrest at Troas because Titus was absent and departure for Macedonia; here arrival in Macedonia still brings no rest and affliction. The locations and spirit/flesh formulations stay distinct.

Titus's arrival brings divine comfort after the earlier account of not finding Titus and having no rest of spirit before departing for Macedonia. This links the letter's absence/arrival narrative without moving the arrival to Troas.

Both describe a returning coworker's report of the recipients' longing bringing comfort to Paul amid affliction. Here the messenger is Titus and the report includes mourning and zeal; Thessalonians names Timothy, faith and love. The communities and messengers differ.

Both reflect on painful correspondence. The earlier unit describes writing with anguish and tears to reveal love rather than cause sorrow; here Paul considers the letter's temporary sorrow and his regret. The link does not identify an unpreserved letter with a particular surviving chapter.

The following explanation distinguishes godly sorrow leading to saving repentance from worldly sorrow leading to death. It gives the specific reason why Paul rejoices over repentance rather than sorrow itself.

Acts depicts hearers cut to the heart receiving Peter's call to repentance, baptism and forgiveness. It illustrates sorrow followed by a saving response related to Paul's principle; it does not name those hearers as the Corinthians or repeat the worldly-sorrow contrast.

The concrete diligence, indignation, fear, longing, zeal and vindication following godly sorrow correspond to John's demand for fruit worthy of repentance. The target calls for evident response but does not reproduce Paul's list or situation.

Both explain a purpose for Paul's writing in terms of the recipients' demonstrated response. The earlier statement concerns proof of obedience; here it concerns their diligence on the speakers' behalf becoming clear before God. No wrongdoer's identity is supplied.

Both connect joy with another person's being refreshed. Corinthians emphasizes comfort and Titus's spirit refreshed by the whole community; Philemon has joy and encouragement because the recipient's love refreshed the saints' hearts. Participants and the spirit/hearts wording remain distinct.

Both connect Paul's boasting about the recipients with whether the claim proves true. The present report concerns Titus and an outcome already experienced; chapter9 concerns boasting to Macedonians and precaution that preparation not prove empty. Their content and time are not conflated.

Both join obedience with fear and trembling. Here Titus remembers how the Corinthians received him; Philippians connects the recipients' obedience with working out salvation. The same phrase is not made an identical instruction or occasion.

Both express confidence about the receiving community. Here Paul rejoices in confidence in the Corinthians; Thessalonians explicitly places confidence in the Lord concerning their doing the instructions. The stated basis and scope differ.

Romans explicitly names Macedonia's willing contribution for the poor saints in Jerusalem. Here Paul introduces grace among Macedonian Churches, continued as generosity and ministry to saints. The named region connects the reports without importing every later detail into this introductory unit.

The Macedonians' deep poverty producing generosity corresponds to Jesus' praise of a poor widow's gift despite its small amount. The widow gives her whole livelihood; the Macedonian report does not state that identical total or identify the givers.

Giving by their own choice corresponds to the later direction that each decide in the heart rather than give under compulsion. The Macedonian example includes beyond-ability giving; the later instruction does not command that amount of everyone.

Sharing in ministry to the saints is later described concretely as service supplying what the saints lack and overflowing in thanksgiving to God. This connects the same collection argument's participation and stated benefit.

Giving themselves first to the Lord corresponds to the appeal to present one's body as a living, holy sacrifice to God. The Macedonian report additionally says to us through God's will; Romans's appeal does not mention that same delegation.

The urging that Titus complete the collection grace corresponds to his diligence and acceptance of the appeal. The earlier beginning is stated here, while the later verses emphasize God-given concern and voluntary response rather than compulsory service.

Both address the Corinthians as rich or abounding in word and knowledge. Here that abundance, alongside faith, diligence and the love from us in you, motivates abounding in the collection grace. The earlier target does not repeat the whole list.

The explicit refusal to speak as a command corresponds to the later rejection of compulsion in giving. Here others' diligence tests love's genuineness; later the giver's heartfelt decision is foregrounded.

Christ's becoming poor for the recipients' enrichment corresponds to His self-emptying, slave-form and obedience unto death. The passages describe gracious self-humbling through different images; Philippians does not literally present the rich/poor contrast.

Both recall the recipients' prior-year readiness. Here Paul says they began both doing and desiring; later he says Achaia was prepared since last year when he boasted to Macedonians. Neither statement removes the present calls to finish and prepare the gift.

Completing the earlier eager desire corresponds to sending brothers to prepare the previously promised gift. Both seek actual readiness; chapter9 adds the contrast between a blessing and something extorted.

Acceptance according to what one has corresponds to Jesus' assessment of the widow's gift relative to her poverty and the others' surplus. Her whole-livelihood gift is not made a universal required amount by this comparison.

The concern for relief without afflicting the givers relates to the community's distribution according to need so that none was needy. Acts narrates property sales and distribution; it does not reproduce Paul's explicit equality/reciprocity argument or impose that scheme here.

Meeting others' lack from available resources corresponds to the believers' sharing and distributing according to need. The Corinthian instruction adds possible reciprocal help from the others' abundance; Acts does not state that later reversal.

Paul quotes the much/no-excess and little/no-shortage result of gathering manna. Exodus describes measurement and each person's gathering for those belonging to his household; Paul applies the saying within his argument for sharing resources. Exodus says no lack where Corinthians says no shortage.

Titus's God-given diligence for the Corinthians corresponds to Timothy's sincere care for the Philippians' circumstances. These are named examples of coworker concern, not the same person or receiving community.

Titus's acceptance of the appeal and voluntary diligence answer the earlier urging that he complete the grace among the recipients. This compares appeal and response without reconstructing an unprinted itinerary from the verb went.

Both describe Titus accompanied by a brother. Here the unnamed brother is praised throughout the Churches; the later passage asks whether Titus exploited the recipients and describes shared conduct. The unnamed companions are not thereby identified as the same individual or as Luke.

The Church-appointed traveling companion for administering the gift corresponds to Paul's plan to send approved representatives with the Corinthians' gift to Jerusalem. The selection wording and stated purposes differ; neither text supplies the unnamed man's identity.

Taking precautions against blame over the administered gift corresponds to Paul's later question whether he exploited the recipients through any messenger. The comparison concerns integrity in delegated ministry, not a concession that misappropriation occurred.

The concern for what is honorable before the Lord and people relates to Proverbs's instruction to take thought for good things before the Lord and people. The wording is related, while the collection-administration application is specific to Corinthians.

The unnamed brother's greater diligence corresponds to Titus's still greater diligence in the same collection mission. The repeated commendation supports the delegation without merging the men or transferring this brother's history of testing to Titus.

Titus's partnership with Paul corresponds to Paul's taking Titus along on the Jerusalem journey with Barnabas. Galatians supplies a named association, not every claim about Titus's current work or the unnamed Church envoys here.

Showing proof of love to the delegates and Churches corresponds to loving in deed and truth rather than word or tongue alone. The collection supplies the particular action in Corinthians; John gives the broader instruction.

The ministry to the saints recalls the Macedonians' request for fellowship in that ministry. The present letter's repetition links the collection argument, without making the Corinthians and Macedonians the same group.

The claim about Achaia's readiness since last year corresponds to the earlier account of beginning to do and desire the gift last year. The statements concern preparation rather than narrating completion of the promised contribution.

The sending precaution that Paul's boasting not prove empty corresponds to the instruction to show proof of love and his boasting before the Churches. Both connect the collection's actual response with the credibility of the commendation.

The possible shame if visiting Macedonians find them unprepared contrasts with Paul's prior boasting to Macedonians of Achaia's readiness. This is the explicit internal risk, not a report that the unprepared visit actually happened.

Both arrange contributions before Paul's arrival. The earlier letter directs regular setting aside so collections need not begin when he comes; here brothers prepare the promised gift as a blessing rather than something extorted. The procedures differ.

Both employ sowing and reaping for corresponding consequences. Corinthians contrasts sparse and generous sowing in the giving argument; Galatians contrasts sowing to flesh or Spirit and persevering in doing good. The types of harvest are not made identical.

Both instruct giving without a grieved heart. Deuteronomy commands giving to the needy brother and connects it with the Lord's blessing; Corinthians adds the giver's heartfelt decision, absence of compulsion and God's love of a cheerful giver.

God's ability to supply sufficiency for good work corresponds to the assurance that God will fill every need according to His riches in glory in Christ Jesus. Philippians's surrounding passage likewise concerns support received, with its own recipients and circumstances.

Both describe giving to the poor and enduring righteousness: Corinthians says scattered abroad and for the age, while the Greek-numbered Psalm111 says scattered gifts and for an age of an age. The Psalm also describes a horn raised in glory, which Paul does not reproduce.

The One supplying seed to the sower and bread for food recalls Isaiah's description of rain or snow making the earth produce seed and bread. Paul develops the provision image into multiplied seed and fruits of righteousness; Isaiah's following analogy concerns God's effective word.

The following because-clause explains how generosity produces thanksgiving through the ministry: it supplies the saints' lack and overflows in many thanksgivings to God. This is an explicit internal cause and result.

Supplying the saints' lack corresponds to the earlier appeal for the recipients' abundance to meet others' lack. Here Paul additionally emphasizes thanksgiving to God, while the earlier instruction also anticipates possible reciprocal support.

Both connect visible good action with people glorifying God. The collection's sharing and confessed obedience to Christ's gospel give the specific occasion here; Matthew speaks of people seeing good works and glorifying the heavenly Father.

The beneficiaries' longing and prayer for the donors corresponds to Paul's longing for the Philippians in Christ Jesus' affection. The surrounding Philippians passage joins grace and prayer; the persons and stated reasons for longing remain distinct.

The closing thanks for God's indescribable gift relates to the collection argument's stated grace of Christ, whose becoming poor benefits the recipients. This compares divine generosity without treating the unnamed gift as an explicitly identified physical contribution.
